rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.5-2.8 and 3: the authors run their own WEAP and AquaCrop simulations for the Chichaoua-Mejjate basin using five Med-CORDEX RCMs under RCP4.5/8.5, with ten management scenarios, and report net precipitation, crop cycle, IWD and unmet-demand results (Tables 5-6, Figures 7-14).
rows.notes: The study is a basin-scale water-balance modelling exercise, not an evaluation of drip irrigation. Drip enters only as Scenario 2 (Section 2.8.4), in which drip adoption on 50% of the PMH area is combined with concreting 70% of earthen canals; the result (Section 3.5: annual demand falls ~4%, unmet demand falls 41%/39%) is a direct consequence of assumed plot efficiencies (60% surface vs 95% drip, Table 3) taken from Le Page et al. 2020, not of any measured drip performance. The scenario output is a future projection (2021-2050) never compared with observations of drip water use in the real system, and the drip effect cannot be separated from the canal-lining effect. Under the rule that a model counts only when its output is compared with measurements, this is not the study's own evidence that drip optimizes water use. Note also the authors state (Section 3.5) that improved efficiency reduces percolation recharge to the aquifer, and that farmers in the drip-irrigated private perimeters over-irrigate because water is free. Q3-Q9 set to no following Q2 = no.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper's own findings concern climate-change impacts on net precipitation, crop cycle length, IWD and unmet demand under WEAP scenarios; drip irrigation is an assumed scenario parameter rather than a studied technology.
